name: Bunkier Sztuki Gallery of Contemporary Art
watch: Krakow councillors voted down the mayor's plan to merge it with the MOCAK museum.

overview: Municipal contemporary art gallery at pl. Szczepański 3a, Krakow (Wikipedia).

Polish Wikipedia dates the institution's history to 1950, when the Bureau of Art Exhibitions (BWA) was created. The gallery received municipal status in 1994 and adopted the name Bunkier Sztuki in 1995.
The building was designed by Krystyna Tołłoczko-Różyska (Polish Wikipedia). English Wikipedia dates its construction to 1965 and credits Stefan Borzęcki and Antoni Hajdecki with the concrete facade.

Directors: Krzysztof Głuchowski (1995 to 1999), Jarosław Suchan (1999 to 2002), Maria Anna Potocka (2002 to 2010 and 2019 to 2024), Piotr Cypryański (2010 to 2014), Magdalena Ziółkowska (2014 to 2018) and Delfina Jałowik (since 2024) (Polish Wikipedia).
The building was under renovation from 2021 to 2024 (Polish Wikipedia). English Wikipedia counts more than 980 exhibitions and a collection of 445 works by 170 artists.
details.funding_verdict: Bunkier Sztuki: mainly public: the City of Krakow
funding: The gallery is financed by the City of Krakow (Polish Wikipedia: "finansowana przez Miasto Kraków").

press.overall: Three pieces from 2019 to 2024 cover the 2019 merger plan, how the city appoints directors, and a 2024 labour court ruling.

items.title: Richard Unwin, "Krakow City Council rejects mayor's plan to merge the city's two leading contemporary art spaces" (29 April 2019)
points: A clear council majority voted on 24 April against Mayor Jacek Majchrowski's plan to combine Bunkier Sztuki with MOCAK under the MOCAK name; MOCAK's director, Potocka, was appointed to lead Bunkier in February and one person runs both.

Artists Monika Drożyńska and Iwona Demko wrote to Culture Minister Piotr Gliński on 3 February, asked for an open competition for the director, and warned of a "detrimental impact on the local, regional and national contemporary art scene." Drożyńska said it was "impossible for one person to ensure the diversity of" the two programmes.
The mayor attributed his plans to a decline in Bunkier's "position and prestige" and in visitor numbers.

items.title: editorial board, "Delfina Jałowik dyrektorką Bunkra Sztuki, czyli w Krakowie bez zmian. Komentarz redakcji" (1 December 2023)
points: The city announced on 30 November 2023 that Jałowik, a long-time MOCAK curator described as Potocka's "prawa ręka" (my translation: right hand), won the director competition. The editors write "wszystko zostaje w rodzinie" (my translation: everything stays in the family) and argue it confirms Bunkier's dependence on MOCAK.

Says a competition announced after Magdalena Ziółkowska's dismissal in 2018 never took place, that Majchrowski appointed Potocka in February 2019 without one, and that the candidates' programmes were not published.

items.title: Katarzyna Kojzar, "Masza Potocka traci stanowisko dyrektorki MOCAK-u. Część pracowników oskarżyła ją o mobbing" (2 October 2024)
points: A national news outlet, not art press. Reports that curator Lidia Krawczyk challenged her dismissal from Bunkier Sztuki in the labour court and that in July 2024 the court found, in the article's quoted words, that the curator was dismissed unlawfully and that Potocka "dopuściła się mobbingu" (my translation: committed mobbing). The article calls the ruling final.
Potocka disputes the verdict. President Aleksander Miszalski announced on 2 October 2024 that she would no longer direct MOCAK.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the gallery is the City of Krakow. The documented points are the 2019 merger plan rejected by the city council, Magazyn Szum's account of Potocka's 2019 appointment without a competition, and the July 2024 labour court finding, reported by OKO.press, that Potocka committed mobbing in a case concerning Bunkier Sztuki.

name: Museum of Islamic Art
records_note: The Museum of Islamic Art has no records of its own; parent Qatar Museums posts no reports, accounts or sponsors but lists eight trustees.
affiliations_note: Overseen by Qatar Museums since its founding, with Mathaf, the National Museum of Qatar, the 3-2-1 Olympic and Sports Museum and Fire Station under the same body.

overview: Museum of Islamic art on an artificial peninsula about 60 metres off the Doha Corniche, in a park of roughly 290,000 square metres, linked to the mainland by two bridges (Wikipedia).

One of the first projects initiated by Qatar Museums (stated by the museum). The then-emir opened it on 22 November 2008 (Wikipedia) and it opened to the public on 1 December 2008 (Bidoun; Wikipedia gives 8 December).
Collection of Islamic art from the 7th to the 20th centuries, from Spain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Turkey, India and Central Asia.

Designed by I. M. Pei, inspired by the fountain of the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo. Limestone exterior, five floors, a central tower and dome. Interiors by Wilmotte Associates. Built by the Turkish firm Baytur.
On site: a library of more than 21,000 books on Islamic art, a cafe and a gift shop (Qatar Living), the IDAM restaurant (Wikipedia) and MIA Park.
Reopened on 5 October 2022 after a ten-month renovation (museum site). Wikipedia counts 18 renovated galleries.

Visiting: open Saturday to Tuesday 9am to 7pm, Thursday 9am to 9pm, Friday 1:30pm to 7pm, closed Wednesday (museum site). Qatar Living (June 2026) gives QAR 50 for non-resident adults, though its FAQ says typically around QAR 100. Free for Qatar residents with ID and children aged 16 and under.
details.funding_verdict: Museum of Islamic Art: state-owned: owned by Qatar Museums, a Qatari government entity; no sponsor or donor named
funding: Two unnamed people close to the situation said the museum's costs are ringfenced while budgets were cut elsewhere, after the emir approved cuts to culture and other budgets in early 2016. Qatar Museums declined to comment on the culture budget (The Art Newspaper, Georgina Adam, 10 March 2016).

red_flags.heading: Gulf state body
points: Status: Qatar Museums is "a Qatari government entity", founded in 2005 and formerly the Qatar Museums Authority (Wikipedia). It operates under the patronage of the Amir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani (Qatar Museums site).

Owner: the museum is owned by Qatar Museums (Wikipedia), which also runs Mathaf and the National Museum of Qatar and is chaired by Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani (Qatar Museums site).

10 March 2016: citing the Financial Times, The Art Newspaper reported that 240 Qatar Museums staff had been let go, leaving fewer than 800 of 1,200 two years earlier. Qatar Museums declined to confirm the figures.

press.overall: Little criticism of the museum as an institution; the critical pieces found concern its displays and the state spending around it.

items.title: Antonia Carver, "Museum of Islamic Art" (2009)
points: The galleries are "almost devoid of information"; labels are minimal and audio guides "offered some description".
Objects are "imbued with power and meaning more through the aesthetics of display than for their place in history"; astrolabes sit on glass shelves "as though it were an installation".
Notes the museum's "Bilbao-inspired brand-building potential" and calls "building bridges" "a hackneyed concept tacked on to nearly every cultural initiative in the Gulf".

items.title: Georgina Adam, "Football outscores culture as Qatar spending slumps" (2016)
points: News report on the 2016 cuts to Qatar Museums, not a critique of the museum; it relies on unnamed sources.

items.title: Sarah El-Richani, "The birth pangs of Qatar's art scene" (2013)
points: Critics questioned how public money was used and where unannounced acquisitions ended up. It does not criticise the Museum of Islamic Art, which it cites as evidence that Qatar Museums cultivated local and regional culture.

wider_context: In 2013, social media users led by a Qatari journalist accused the Qatar Museums Authority of corruption, mismanagement and nepotism (openDemocracy, Sarah El-Richani).

The same article says some Qataris active on social media lamented Damien Hirst's sculptures, and gives two explanations for why Abdessemed's film "Printemps" was not shown at Mathaf: social media reports that Sheikha Mayassa intervened, and officials citing technical issues.
The museum is owned by Qatar Museums, the body these accusations name.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is Qatari state money channelled through Qatar Museums, with no private or corporate funder named in any source found. The weak points are the lack of published accounts or budget and the museum's place inside a state body. Worth watching: whether Qatar Museums publishes accounts or a sponsor list.

name: Misk Art Institute
funding: Subsidiary of the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation (Misk), a non-profit the Crown Prince founded in 2011.
watch: Founded December 2017; Ahmed Mater was its director then. Its summer 2026 show at Prince Faisal bin Fahd Arts Hall has over 40 works.
why_flagged: Subsidiary of the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation (Misk), a non-profit the Crown Prince founded in 2011.
records_note: Its parent Misk Foundation lists annual reports for 2019 to 2024.
affiliations_note: Misk Art Institute is a subsidiary of the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation (Misk). Member of Res Artis.

overview: Non-profit arts organisation in Riyadh running residencies, training, a grant, Misk Art Week and exhibitions, mainly at the Prince Faisal bin Fahd Arts Hall (Misk Art Institute website).

Established in December 2017 by the Misk Foundation, which Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman founded in 2011 (Misk Art Institute website, Wikipedia). Artist Ahmed Mater was its founding director (The Art Newspaper, 2017).

The hall was established in 1985 by royal decree of King Fahd as the Fine Arts Hall, later named for Prince Faisal bin Fahd. It covers 5,600 square metres and reopened under the Institute at the end of 2019 (Arab News, 31 December 2019).
The Institute has been the commissioner of Saudi Arabia's national pavilion at the Venice Biennale since 2018 (Arab News).
The site gives directions to the hall but no visitor details.
details.funding_verdict: Misk Art Institute: state-linked: subsidiary of the Misk Foundation, founded by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
funding: The Institute describes itself as affiliated with the non-profit Mohammed bin Salman Foundation "Misk" (Misk Art Institute website).

red_flags.heading: Gulf state patronage
points: 8 December 2017: The Art Newspaper reported that the Crown Prince launched the Institute as the artistic arm of his Misk Foundation, with Mater as director (Anna Somers Cocks).

January 2018: at the launch of Misk's international programme at MoMA, Mater described the approach as "instructed by the Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud". Rijin Sahakian wrote that the Crown Prince personally appointed Mater (Hyperallergic, 1 November 2018).
31 December 2019: Arab News reported that Culture Minister Prince Badr bin Abdullah, who chairs the Institute, patronised the reopening of the Prince Faisal bin Fahd Arts Hall.

red_flags.heading: Institutions declined Misk money after the Khashoggi killing
points: October 2018: Misk had planned to fully fund the Brooklyn Museum exhibition "Syria, Then and Now", which opened on 13 October, and a Met seminar on collecting the Middle East; both museums paid for them themselves. The Met's cost was under USD 20,000 (Hyperallergic, Jasmine Weber, 18 October 2018).

Columbia University announced that Mater's lecture of 22 October 2018 would not take place, and the Middle East Institute withdrew from the Arab Art and Education Initiative (Hyperallergic, 18 October 2018). The Art Newspaper reported on 30 October 2018 that Misk had suspended its foreign programme.
November 2018: the Gates Foundation suspended its planned engagement with the Misk Foundation, calling the killing "extremely troubling" (Wikipedia).

press.overall: Criticism is limited to pieces from October and November 2018, after the Khashoggi killing; none after 2018 was found.

items.title: Rijin Sahakian, "A Coalition of The Willing: How Saudi Arabia and US Arts Institutions Partnered on a Cultural Diplomacy Offensive" (2018)
points: Argues Misk is presented as grassroots but was created and chaired by the Crown Prince, who personally appointed Mater; says The Art Newspaper quoted Stephen Stapleton at length without disclosing his Misk role as director of international programmes.

Argues the Met and Brooklyn Museum acted too late, having long known the kingdom's record, and that positive press from Sotheby's and The Art Newspaper helped rebrand the Crown Prince as a reformer. Names the Institute at length.

items.title: Jasmine Weber, "Several Major New York Art Institutions Step Away from Saudi-Funded Initiatives" (2018)
points: News report, not an essay: lists the museums that took over funding Misk had planned, the Columbia lecture that would not take place and the Middle East Institute's withdrawal.

items.title: Anna Somers Cocks, with a comment from Stephen Stapleton, "Do not penalise Saudi Arabian artists for the murder of Jamal Khashoggi" (30 October 2018)
points: Argues Saudi artists should not be punished for the killing and that fear and self-censorship among them have grown.
Names the Institute and Mater but does not criticise either; it says the killing forced the West to reassess its view of the Crown Prince.

items.title: Anna Somers Cocks, "Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince adds art and culture to his portfolio" (8 December 2017)
points: Not criticism: describes the Institute's plans; no budget or funders stated.

details.bottom_line: The Institute is a subsidiary of the Crown Prince's foundation, chaired by the culture minister in 2019, with no budget, accounts or donor list published. The weak points are that opacity and the October 2018 withdrawals of Western partners after the Khashoggi killing. Worth watching: whether it publishes accounts.

name: Moderna Galerija (MG+MSUM)
funding: National museum funded by the Slovenian Ministry of Culture.
why_flagged: Slovenian Ministry of Culture: up to EUR 2.07m from the state budget for its 2022 programme, plus up to EUR 100,000 for the Venice Biennale pavilion.
records_note: Its public-information page posts annual reports 2020 to 2024 in the AJPES finance format and names the council.
finances_note: FY2024 income EUR 2.69M; on the cash statement of EUR 2.64M, about 91 percent is state budget and EU funds, 8 percent other non-tax revenue (annual report pp. 57-58).
affiliations_note: Runs the Museum of Contemporary Art Metelkova as its second site, handed its Graphic Biennale to MGLC in 1985, and lists Slovenian museums, two universities and L'Internationale as partners. Member of L'Internationale.

overview: Slovenia's national museum of modern and contemporary art, on two sites in Ljubljana: MG+ (Moderna galerija) at Cankarjeva 15 and +MSUM (Museum of Contemporary Art Metelkova) at Maistrova 3 (museum website).
Established by a decree of the government of the People's Republic of Slovenia on 30 December 1947 and opened to the public on 3 January 1948 (Wikipedia).
The main building was designed by Edvard Ravnikar and completed in 1948. The Metelkova museum opened as an expansion on 26 November 2011 (Wikipedia).
The collection covers Slovenian art of the 20th and 21st centuries with works by foreign artists. The museum also runs debate, documentation, education and research programmes (Wikipedia).
Zdenka Badovinac directed the museum from 1993 until 2020 (Apollo).
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm. Thursdays in July and August until 8 pm (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Moderna galerija (MG+MSUM): public: a national museum whose founder is the Slovenian Ministry of Culture
funding: The Ministry of Culture, as the founder of Moderna galerija, issued the call for applications for the post of director (CIMAM, text of 10 March 2022).

red_flags.heading: Ministry of Culture and the director's post
points: Apollo (Dorian Batycka, 23 December 2020): the ministry advertised Zdenka Badovinac's post three times and in November 2020 named the poet and art historian Robert Simonisek (spelling as in Apollo) as interim director. Badovinac called her removal "absolutely political". The ministry rejected the criticism, saying that appointing new directors has been routine under left-wing governments for decades.

CIMAM, in an unsigned text posted on 10 March 2022 beside the staff letter and written in the staff's voice: after Badovinac's mandate ended in 2020 the ministry repeated the call for the post three times instead of reappointing her; it changed the museum's statutes despite "loudly voiced opposition" from the professional public and changed the qualifications for the post. The text says these changes were made to enable the appointment of the ministry's "favoured candidate", Aleš Vaupotič, and calls it one of many "politically motivated changes" of directors. Badovinac had reapplied.

Staff letter of 8 March 2022, addressed to the Government and the Ministry of Culture: 27 employees, 79.4 percent of all employees according to the letter, demanded the resignation or dismissal of Vaupotič. Their grievances: he removed part of the permanent exhibition without notifying its curators, mishandled contracts of external help and part-time employees, approved inflated budgets and pressured employees.

press.overall: The criticism in art and museum media concerns political control of the museum's leadership between 2020 and 2022, not its funding sources.

items.title: Dorian Batycka, "Concerns rise about cultural freedom in Slovenia" (23 December 2020)
points: Reports concern about cultural freedom under the ruling Slovenian Democratic Party led by Janez Janša, naming Badovinac's removal from Moderna galerija.
Matevž Čelik says two of the three jurors selecting his successor were appointed by the ruling party and that earlier experience requirements were dropped.
The ministry rejects the criticism.

items.title: "A Courageous Action by the staff of Moderna galerija, Ljubljana" (10 March 2022)
points: CIMAM's Museum Watch Committee introduces the staff's public letter of protest of 8 March 2022 asking the Government and the Ministry of Culture for Vaupotič's resignation or dismissal.
The ministry's repeated call and statute changes are described in the unsigned text beside the letter, which gives the staff's account.

wider_context: Apollo: opposition member of parliament Violeta Tomić, acting head of the parliamentary culture committee, cites the cancelling of major subsidies for the public broadcaster and of financing for film production, and the firing of directors of several major cultural institutions.

Apollo: an open letter of 17 November 2020 to Culture Minister Vasko Simoniti, with more than 1,000 signatures, criticised the director replacements and called the planned Museum of Slovenian Independence a "propaganda institution". The government said in a press release of 13 December that these characterisations were incorrect and that the museum would be curated by professional historians with no political affiliations.
The letter's criticism of director replacements concerns the ministry that founded Moderna galerija and issued the call for its director.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is the state: a national museum founded by the Slovenian Ministry of Culture. The documented issue is the ministry's handling of the director's post from 2020 to 2022: Badovinac called her removal "absolutely political", museum staff described politically motivated changes in a 2022 letter and accompanying text, and the ministry said that replacing directors is routine under left-wing governments.

name: Alternative Space LOOP
funding: Non-profit association (2019); 2026 shows supported by Arts Council Korea, supervised by Seoul Metropolitan Government, plus individual LOOP's Friends donors.
watch: Dec 2025 Euljiro move drew a public gentrification inquiry from Cheonggyecheon-Euljiro Preservation Alliance and others.
records_note: Its Support page names its chairs, directors, auditor and 44 individual donors, undated.

overview: Non-profit art space in Seoul. E-flux notices from 2024 and 2026 give its address as 3rd Floor, 172-1 Cheonggyecheon-ro, Jung District. K-ARTNOW (23 December 2025) reports a move to the first floor of the same address, along the Cheonggyecheon stream, and a reopening on 16 December 2025.
Opened in 1999 in the Hongdae area of Seoul and is described as Korea's first alternative space (e-flux directory). K-ARTNOW says it was founded in Mapo-gu, Seoul.
Became a non-profit organisation in 2019 for its 20th anniversary. It has nine board members and eighty general members (e-flux directory).
Director Ji Yoon Yang joined as a curator in 2006 and became director in autumn 2017 (Whitewall, Katy Donoghue, 20 November 2024).

Programme: exhibitions, an annual open call for artists and independent curators, and research and workshops. Its 2026 to 2027 mission statement says it will challenge the financialisation of art and use feminist and communal approaches (K-ARTNOW).
Visiting: Monday to Sunday, 10 am to 7 pm. Activities are free and open to everyone (e-flux).
funding: Director Yang says board members and other members sponsor LOOP monthly, which she says makes it more stable; she calls it a middle-sized organisation with a stronger public role than at the start (Whitewall, 2024).

red_flags.heading: Public questionnaire over the Euljiro move
points: On 15 December 2025 the Cheonggyecheon-Euljiro Preservation Alliance, Listen to the City and the Feminist Designer Social Club posted an open questionnaire on Instagram asking LOOP to answer publicly (K-ARTNOW, 23 December 2025). The questionnaire was addressed to LOOP.

The groups say Sanlim-dong, where LOOP moved, is one of the few remaining metal manufacturing clusters in Euljiro and faces redevelopment and gentrification, and that cultural spaces can speed up gentrification.
They ask for LOOP's reasons for moving, its consideration for local residents and the existing trades, and its stance on gentrification.
In its 2026 to 2027 mission statement LOOP pledges not to use Euljiro's workshops, labour, housing or redevelopment tensions as "cultural material" (stated by the space, via K-ARTNOW).

press.overall: One piece of coverage reports a public challenge to the space; no critic's review criticising the institution was found. The other piece is an interview with the director.

items.title: "A Team", "Korea's First-Generation Alternative Space 'Alternative Space LOOP' Moves to Euljiro" (2025, published 23 December)
points: Reports the questionnaire above on gentrification and the move, alongside LOOP's own mission statement.
Reports the questioners' arguments, not its own.
Title translated from Korean.

items.title: Katy Donoghue, interview with Ji Yoon Yang (2024)
points: Not criticism: an interview of 20 November 2024 in which Yang describes how the 2008 financial crisis forced LOOP to reshape nearly everything to survive, and how the pandemic closed it.

details.bottom_line: LOOP is a small non-profit sustained by monthly contributions from board members and other members. Its weak point is the public challenge over its December 2025 move to Euljiro. Worth watching: LOOP's answer to the December 2025 questionnaire about gentrification in Euljiro.

name: Busan Biennale
funding: 2026 edition run by the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee for Busan Metropolitan City, with BNK Busan Bank and Danish and UK cultural funds.
records_note: It posts yearly public-interest settlement filings for 2023 to 2025 and names its officers and auditors.
affiliations_note: The 2026 edition is run by the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee and held at Busan Museum of Contemporary Art, a former school and a former warehouse. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: International contemporary art biennale held in Busan in even-numbered years. It began in 1998 when the Busan Youth Biennale, the Sea Art Festival and the Busan Outdoor Sculpture Symposium merged, and was earlier called the Pusan International Contemporary Art Festival (Wikipedia). The City of Busan's own page dates its origin to the Busan Youth Biennale of 1981 and says it took its current name after the organizing committee was established in 2000.
Presented by Busan Metropolitan City in cooperation with the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee (Busan Metropolitan City).

The 2026 edition, "Dissident Chorus", runs from 29 August to 1 November 2026 with 46 artists and collectives from 22 countries, directed by Evelyn Simons and Amal Khalaf, who were chosen through an open call that drew over 70 teams (Busan Metropolitan City).
Venues in 2026: Busan Museum of Contemporary Art on Eulsukdo, plus Space OneZ, a marine warehouse on Yeongdo, and the former Busan Nam High School (e-flux, Busan Metropolitan City).
Earlier venues have included the Busan Museum of Modern Art, the Busan Museum of Art, beaches and F1963, a former KISWIRE factory in Suyeong that hosted the 2016 main exhibition (Wikipedia).

Open daily 10:00 to 18:00 except Mondays. The Busan Museum of Contemporary Art charges 16,000 won for adults, Space OneZ and the former Busan Nam High School are free, and a free shuttle links the three venues (Busan Metropolitan City).
details.funding_verdict: Busan Biennale: public body: presented by Busan Metropolitan City with its Organizing Committee
funding: Busan Metropolitan City presents the 2026 biennale in cooperation with the Busan Biennale Organizing Committee (Busan Metropolitan City); Wikipedia states the biennale is hosted by the city and the Organizing Committee.

press.overall: One review of the 2026 edition calls it uneven; it criticises the curation, not the funding or governance.

items.title: Adeline Chia, review of Busan Biennale 2026, "Dissident Chorus" (29 September 2026)
points: Calls it "an uneven biennial, more conceptually focused and powerful in its off-sites" than at the main venue.
Writes that the curation at the Busan Museum of Contemporary Art "feels more staid and generic," citing familiar tropes and "a few needlessly large installations for visual drama."
Says the biennial's open celebration of underdogs and dissent makes it "an accidental foil to the political quarrels plaguing the concurrent Gwangju Biennale."
Criticises the curation, not the institution or its funders.

details.bottom_line: The biennale is presented by Busan Metropolitan City in cooperation with its Organizing Committee. The published review of the 2026 edition, by Adeline Chia in e-flux Criticism, concerns the curation.

name: Sejong Center for the Performing Arts
funding: The Asia Economy interview read did not give the total budget or funding sources; it says the six resident arts groups account for 42% of the budget.
watch: A performing arts centre in Gwanghwamun run with six resident groups (traditional orchestra, dance, choir, musical, theatre, opera); Ahn Hosang became president in 2021.
records_note: The page read showed no published accounts.

overview: A performing arts centre in central Seoul with six resident arts groups (Asia Economy, 20 October 2022).
Its president Ahn Hosang, a former director of the National Theater, was marking one year in office in October 2022 (Asia Economy).
What is there: Korean traditional orchestra, dance, choir, musical, theatre and opera groups; the groups handled 90% of that spring's performances (Asia Economy).
Archive: the page read did not mention an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Sejong Center: public body, funding not itemised in the page read
funding: The resident groups take 42% of the total budget; their audiences were 12.3% of the total in the three years before Ahn took office (Asia Economy, 20 October 2022). The total budget and its sources were not given.
details.bottom_line: The page read gives shares but not amounts or the funder. Seoul city is the likely funder but the page did not say so.

name: Museo Nacional de Escultura
funding: The site identifies the museum as part of the Ministerio de Cultura of the Government of Spain. The pages read did not state a budget or amounts.
watch: State museum of Spanish sculpture on three sites in Valladolid, including the Colegio de San Gregorio.
records_note: The pages read did not link published accounts.

overview: State museum with three sites: Palacio de Villena, Casa del Sol and the Colegio de San Gregorio, Cadenas de San Gregorio, 47011 Valladolid (museum website).

What is there: collection areas listed as Spanish sculpture, artistic reproductions, "Not only sculpture" and documentary heritage; a room on Alonso Berruguete's Mannerism; current exhibitions on the Ribalta family, Salzillo and Gondomar (museum website). The pages read gave no object count.
Archive: the site lists documentary heritage as a collection area; the pages read did not describe it further (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Escultura: state museum; the pages read did not state amounts
funding: Part of the Ministerio de Cultura (museum website). No reporting found of its budget, sponsors or income in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: A State museum paid through the Ministry; the pages read give no figures.

name: TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes
funding: The pages read did not state who funds TEA or in what amounts.
watch: An arts centre in a building by the Swiss architects Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron with the Canarian architect Virgilio Gutiérrez, holding a main collection, the Óscar Domínguez collection and the Isla de Tenerife photography centre collection.

overview: An arts centre in Santa Cruz de Tenerife in a building designed by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron with Virgilio Gutiérrez, using diagonal elements and sloping floors so that public space flows into the building and its courtyard (TEA website).
What is there: the site lists a main collection, the Óscar Domínguez collection and the Isla de Tenerife photography centre collection; the page read does not describe their contents (TEA website).
Archive: the site lists a Centro de Documentación y Biblioteca de Arte; the page read gives no holdings or access details (TEA website).
details.funding_verdict: TEA Tenerife: funders not stated in the pages read.
funding: The page read does not say who funds TEA, including whether the Cabildo de Tenerife does. No reporting found of amounts in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The pages read do not show who pays for TEA or how much; the next step is its transparency section or the Cabildo's accounts.

name: Konsthall C
funding: Region Stockholm gives SEK 300,000 a year for 2025 and 2026, after SEK 250,000 in 2024. The City of Stockholm and the Swedish Arts Council also fund it.

overview: Non-profit exhibition space in a former communal laundry at Cigarrvägen 14 in Hökarängen, a suburb of southern Stockholm (e-flux listing; Creative Time Summit page).

Began in 2004 as a public artwork by the artist Per Hasselberg, made with local community organisations (Creative Time Summit page). It describes itself as "an experiment in urban renewal" and has grown from an artist-run project space into what it calls "an established contemporary art platform" (e-flux call for applications, 20 May 2023).

Programme: several exhibition spaces, an artist-in-residence platform, a citizens' archive and a network of local artists (e-flux call). Kunstkritikk (Hans Carlsson, 5 February 2015) writes that the venue has long focused on Hökarängen, with attention to social planning and the history of the Swedish welfare state.

Directors named in the press: Jens Strandberg and Jenny Richards from 2015, succeeding Karolin Tampere (Kunstkritikk, 2015). Ulrika Flink as artistic director and Erik Annerborn as managing director in 2023, when a three-year artistic directorship for 2024 to 2026 was advertised (e-flux call).
Legal form: the association Kulturföreningen Konsthall C (Region Stockholm decision, 16 September 2025).
Open Thursday to Sunday, 12:00 to 17:00 (e-flux listing).
details.funding_verdict: Konsthall C: public support: Region Stockholm operating grant
funding: Region Stockholm's Kulturförvaltningen granted Kulturföreningen Konsthall C operating support (verksamhetsstöd) of SEK 300,000 for 2025, plus an extra payment of SEK 73,896 decided on 16 September 2025 (delegation decision 37/2025, KN 2025/1082).
not_related: Bonniers Konsthall, a separate art institution at Torsgatan 19 in Stockholm, whose website ties its vision to Jeanette Bonnier. Konsthall C is a different organisation, the association Kulturföreningen Konsthall C in Hökarängen.
details.bottom_line: Konsthall C is a non-profit association in a former laundry in Hökarängen. The funding documented on a page is Region Stockholm operating support of SEK 300,000 for 2025 plus SEK 73,896 extra.
